topic.claim: mutual funds vs the plot back home

paragraphs: A dad saw his son's portfolio and said sell half, buy a plot back home. He wasn't being dumb. He was being smart.
Swipe to read →
I used to think this was old people being scared of risk. It isn't.
A 27-year-old in Bangalore has put everything into SIPs for four years. The portfolio keeps growing. He's proud.
He tells his parents. He's expecting at least a "wah beta".
Instead dad goes quiet. He says the whole thing could vanish overnight. Buy a plot back home.
Try to win this with a returns chart and you will lose. Every time. Because dad isn't arguing about returns.
A plot has a boundary wall. Relatives drive past it. Your chacha knows where it is.
It comes up when your cousin's rishta is discussed. It's wealth the town can verify.
Your Groww screen? Nobody knows it exists except you.
But the real thing underneath isn't showing off either.
In Indian families, whoever owns the assets makes the decisions. Always been this way.
The house is in papa's name. The land is in papa's name. So papa decides where you study and who you marry.
Your portfolio is the first serious money in the family that doesn't need papa's name. Or his permission.
Which is why the counter-offer is never "invest a bit less". It's always a plot.
A plot pulls the money back where the family can see it. Back to the town you left.
It's also a reason to keep coming back. You'll go see it, pay someone, sign papers.
So the market isn't the risk your parents are worried about.
They're looking at the first generation whose money and decisions don't pass through home anymore. The scary part isn't you'll lose the money.
It's that you won't need them to keep it.
And if you're building in fintech, this is your real competition. Not other apps. A plot their father can drive past on a Sunday.

hook_candidates.hook: Your parents don't want you to buy a plot because markets are risky. They want it because a plot keeps your money where they can see it.
A dad saw his son's portfolio and said sell half, buy a plot back home. He wasn't being dumb. He was being smart.
The plot your father wants you to buy isn't an investment. It's a leash with a boundary wall.
Your SIP beats a plot on every chart. So why does your dad still want you to sell up and buy land back home?
Show an Indian parent your portfolio and they'll tell you to sell half for a plot nobody will ever build on. Every time.

paragraphs: There's a fight happening in almost every Indian family where the kid has a decent job in a metro, and it always starts the same way.
Kid shows parents the mutual fund portfolio. Parents call it gambling.
I used to think this was just old people being scared of risk. It isn't.
Swipe to read →

It usually goes like this. A 27-year-old in Bangalore has been putting basically everything into SIPs for four years. The portfolio crosses 25 lakhs. He's proud, he tells his parents, he's expecting at least a "wah beta".
Instead dad goes quiet and then says the whole thing could vanish overnight. Take out 15 lakhs. Buy a plot back home. Or put it in an FD in mummy's name.
If you try to win this argument with a returns chart, you will lose. Every single time. Because dad isn't actually arguing about returns.
A plot has a boundary wall. Relatives drive past it. Your chacha knows exactly where it is. It comes up when your cousin's rishta is being discussed. It's wealth the whole town can verify.
Your Groww screen? Nobody even knows it exists except you.
But it took me a while to see the real thing underneath, and it's not about showing off either.

In Indian families, whoever owns the assets makes the decisions. Always has been that way. The house is in papa's name, the land is in papa's name, so papa decides where you study, who you marry, when you're "settling down".
Your portfolio is the first serious money in the family that doesn't need papa's name on it. Or his permission.
Which is why the counter-offer is never "invest a bit less". It's always a plot. Back home. Or an FD in mom's name.

Both of those pull the money back where the family can see it, and back to the town you left. And honestly, a plot is also a reason for you to keep coming back. You'll have to go see it, pay someone to look after it, sign papers. It ties you to home.
So yeah, the market isn't the risk your parents are worried about.
They're looking at the first generation of Indians whose money, life and decisions don't have to pass through home anymore. And the scary part for them isn't that you'll lose the 25 lakhs.
It's that you won't need them to keep it.
And if you're building anything in fintech in India, this is your real competition. Not the other apps. A plot of land in someone's hometown that their father can drive past on a Sunday.
